articles.text: Despite crime trends, he sees significant progress in town Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers presented his quarterly crime report at the city council meeting on Monday, November 20, noting that despite higher than usual crime items, significant progress is being made toward decreasing crime rates and pursuing criminals. Chief Bowers began with a recap of this year’s crime statistics through the 3rd quarter. Compared with the same time period last year, he noted that crime in Piedmont has increased in nearly every category, including robbery, assault, burglary, theft, and vehicle thefts. “This is no surprise to the council,” said Bowers. “This was the trend that we were seeing during my report in September, where we saw increases in everything from robberies to burglaries, and most notably in larceny theft and vehicle burglary or vehicle theft.” “Unfortunately that trend is continuing,” he said. Additionally, vehicle thefts are up “quite a bit,” according to Bowers. Sixty-two vehicle thefts have taken place in Piedmont this year, a fact Bowers attributes to the vulnerabilities of cars by manufacturers like as Kia and Audi. These cars lack a useful anti-theft device called an immobilizer, which prevents a vehicle from starting when the driver attempts to use a key or key fob that doesn’t match the car. Bowers also admitted that there are dimensions of danger not captured by the raw numbers of his statistics. Speaking about failure to yield incidents specifically, Bowers said, “I have anecdotally seen the behavior of individuals involved in this criminal activity [...] becoming more and more dangerous. They’re literally crashing their vehicles into our vehicles without any regard for our officers’ safety.” Bowers was referring to an incident on November 15, 2023, when the driver of a Kia intentionally struck two police cars on Somerset Road before becoming lodged on the roadway. There was some good news, however. Catalytic converter thefts were significantly down. “In July, we had one catalytic converter theft in the city. In August, we had four. In September, we had none,” said Bowers. For reference, Piedmont has experienced 59 catalytic converter thefts in total this year. articles.text: How can we call America a representative democracy when, at every census, state lawmakers scheme to make peoples’ votes irrelevant? Redistricting, a task which long ago was fair and practical, has been manipulated into a vicious opportunity to cast the opposing party (and its voters) into political irrelevancy. State officials jump at any chance to increase their party’s influence and disadvantage the other at the expense of voters. Reversely, some states have done away with partisan redistricting, and moved to entrusting independent commissions with the task. These commissions are theoretically unbiased, allowing them to draw compact, logical districts, untainted from politics. But these maps draw outcry from state bureaucrats, who will nitpick in an attempt to de-legitimize them. The truth is, drawing a district which pleases everyone is an impossible task. Most Americans live in political clusters which are either incredibly Republican or Democratic. Firstly, this makes it easy for officials to exploit these clusters to their advantage. Secondly, anyone who tries drawing a fair district is in for a tough time. Equal numbers of opposing voters often results in a snakeshaped district in an attempt to include both parties, but which diminishes geographical representation. Drawing a compact district typically results in it being onesided, leaving dissenting voters unheard. If one doesn’t factor race into districting, minorities may be unrepresented entirely. On the other hand, if one tries to make districts fully diverse, minority voices might get diluted. There are few, yet notable guidelines for redistricting. Firstly, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed discriminatory districts. The VRA is effective in protecting minorities, yet there is little legislation for political interference. Constitutional law itself implies that districts should be compact, competitive, and maintain historical political boundaries. Our Founding Fathers’ original vision for redistricting has been dumbed down into an ugly skirmish for political traction. Nate Woodley is a senior at Piedmont High School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 15. articles.text: In November the U.S. will celebrate Native American Heritage Month. This month presents a special opportunity to honor Indigenous cultures and contributions. As with the rest of North America – also known as Turtle Island to some tribes – Piedmont itself sits on Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homes. More specifically, Piedmont occupies the traditional homelands of Ohlone peoples, including the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe and Confederated Villages of Lisjan. Before the arrival of European settlers, these tribes were stewards of this land for thousands of years. Indigenous people have been leaders in reintroducing buffalo in Montana, restoring salmon populations in the Columbia River, and protecting sacred land at Standing Rock in the Dakotas. In California, prescribed burning is a long-standing Indigenous practice that diminishes wildfire risk. The state government opposed this practice in the past, but today prescribed burns are once again a key element of the State’s approach to forest management and wildfire risk reduction. Many Indigenous activists lead the climate movement. At age 21, Xiya Bastida, co-founder of the Re-Earth Initiative, earned a spot in Time Magazine’s Next list for her climate justice activism. Other prominent Indigenous activists include Tara Houska, Quannah Chasinghorse, Winona LaDuke, Siqiñiq Maupin, and Dallas Goldtooth. Here in the East Bay, Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, works with Native and non-native communities to revitalize lost cultural knowledge and caretaking practices on land across the East Bay. Indigenous people in the U.S. have the highest poverty rate among all minority groups (25.4%), and the highest mortality rates for many preventable illnesses, resulting in a life expectancy that is 5.5 years lower than the national average. It indicates that Indigenous people are disproportionately impacted by climate change. In his proclamation of National Native American Heritage Month, President Biden called on all Americans to celebrate November 24 as “Native American Heritage Day.” I encourage all Piedmonters to spend some time on Friday reading or listening to Indigenous voices by visiting the official websites for the Muwékma Ohlone Tribe (www.muwekma.org) and Confederated Villages of Lisjan (www.villagesoflisjan.org) or viewing the following podcasts: Indigenous Earth Community Podcast, Good Fire, and Indigenous Climate Action Pod. Alyssa Romea is an AmeriCorps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division.

Oakland Zoo welcomes 2 mountain lion cubs By Jay Russell Oakland Zoo has two new star attractions – a pair of young, orphaned mountain lion siblings. They were rescued and transported to Oakland Zoo on November 14 by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife following a search for the kittens. Given the names Maple and Willow by the zoo’s staff, they mark the 25th and 26th mountain lion rescues at the zoo since the program started in 2017. Both kittens are female, approximately six to ten weeks old, and each weighed roughly five pounds upon arrival. An adult female mountain lion, who CDFW believes is their mother, was struck by a car and killed on Saturday, November 11, along Highway 280, near the Hillsboro-Burlingame area. Over the weekend, residents reported seeing two cubs alone near the area, and they were found safe in the backyard of one of reporting residents. When the cubs arrived at Oakland Zoo, the Veterinary Hospital staff conducted a thorough health examination of both cubs. The exam included virus testing, parasite treatment, and bloodwork testing. Additionally, vital fluids were administered to the visibly dehydrated kittens. Although underweight and dehydrated, they showed no signs of extreme illness. “Our team will be caring for the cubs daily to restore them to full health and for their overall animal well-being,” said Dr. Alex Herman, Oakland Zoo’s Vice President of Veterinary Services. Orphaned kittens remain on average for eight days in the Zoo’s ICU. Once cleared, they are moved to a holding area at Vet Hospital for weeks until CDFW identifies a proper permanent home for the cubs. On Thanksgiving, Willow and Maple were skewer-fed by keepers to help them get used to people. According to the zoo, Maple has had no trouble with skewer feeding and has been eating like a champ, while Willow is still adjusting to her new diet and how to eat it. In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because the cubs are so young, they lack those skills and cannot return to the wild. “These cubs became orphans when their mother was struck by a car on a busy highway, a tragedy suffered by wildlife when safe passage across their natural territories isn’t possible. We support and advocate for more wildlife crossings, such as the one opened in Santa Cruz earlier this year on Highway 17,” said Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia. In 2012, the Oakland Zoo participated in a training session focused on resolving conflicts between humans and wildlife. This training led to forming BACAT (Bay Area Cougar Action Team). The alliance brings together various agencies, nonprofit organizations, local parks, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, and mountain lion researchers. articles.text: Piedmont’s bus riders may need to rethink their commuting plans in the near future. AC Transit met with Piedmont City Council on November 20 to discuss proposed changes to bus routes 18, 33, and 88. AC Transit proposes to eliminate Line 33 and split its services between Lines 18 and 88. Under this new plan, Line 18 would travel down Park Boulevard, across Lake Merritt, and then on Broadway to 20th Street in downtown Oakland, before continuing along the current Line 18 to Berkeley and Albany via Martin Luther King Jr. Way. Line 88 would replace the current line 33 service along Oakland Avenue and Harrison Street, with rides between Piedmont, downtown Oakland, and downtown Berkeley. In addition, AC Transit is also seeking riders’ input on the bus network’s larger goals, asking riders if they prefer a bus system that focuses on a more far-reaching service and more bus stops, or one that has lower wait times and more frequent service. Members of the public may voice their opinion on the proposed changes at AC Transit’s online open house event on December 7. Residents can also visit any Oakland Public Library branch for more information or to submit feedback on the decision. “It’s important now to share this information with your colleagues, your neighbors, your family and friends, and your constituents to ensure that their voices are heard,” said Maria Henderson, External Affairs Representative with AC Transit. AC Transit intends to vote on proposed changes to its bus network in April 2024. For more information visit www.actransit. org/realign. articles.text: It’s the time of year when gift giving is top of mind, especially for parents searching for toy ideas for their tots. Since play provides the foundation for robust learning, many parents are looking for toys that will be fun as well as infused with learning potential. How do we evaluate the quality of a toy in terms of a beneficial learning edge as well as the fun factor? What do we look for in a toy? We can look to the research for a few guiding principles. Regarding quantity, research shows that a bit less is best. For some children, the overload of all the play items can be overwhelming and distracting, causing the child to pick up one toy, drop it and move on. Regarding quality, research would have us remember the value of the simple “open-ended” toy which can be used in multiple ways. For example, hardwood blocks can be for building, or a make-believe car, or pretend food. Conversely, “closed-ended” toys (which consumers tend to gravitate toward when gift giving) tend to have a “right way” to play, and include such toys as a cash register, Mr. Potato Head, or Legos. Beyond these general principles of quantity and quality, what should be our toy buying guide? To foster problem solving, look to toys such as blocks, instruments or simple board games (or consider keys and containers with lids which you do not have to purchase). To tap into the child’s experimental tendencies, Kids having fun at home consider toys such as a sand or water table (or look to flashlights, colanders, or a whisk to use in the bath which you do not have to purchase). To encourage communication, doll houses and books are excellent choices. You can introduce dress up or rhyming games for similar effects without a price tag. Cognitive development can be fun with toy items such as matching/memory and sorting picture cards, but can also be enjoyed with sorting of silverware, clothing or small household items using a muffin tin for a non-retail option. Creative kids will enjoy gifts of silly putty, paint or other art supplies, and tape, paper towel rolls, paper plates and cotton balls can also be creative fun without additional purchases. Motor development can be enhanced with gifts such as puzzles, balls and shape sorters. And don’t forget that the same fun and developmental stimulation can be had with common kitchen items such as measuring cups, mixing bowls, plastic cups, etc. Regarding social/emotional-based toys, dolls and puppets can’t be beat, and a mirror can do the trick for no purchase. Collaborative toys are always a good idea, such as a construction set or play kitchen. If you want to get the same effect without the specific toy purchase, the laundry basket, sheets and pillows can become a wonderful collaborative fort building experience. Have a wonderful gift-giving season. PHS junior Clare Weiss, a member of the All-State Jazz Choir, will be a soloist on the jazz standard “Misty” by Errol Garner. articles.text: In the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) league, fall is referred to as the “off season” to contrast the intensity of the build-and-competition season from January through April. But, Highlander Robotics is not off; in fact, this is the busiest time for our outreach projects. We learn a lot when we build our robot each year and through outreach, we leverage our technical skills to teach others and to do service projects. I’d like to share information about the outreach partnerships we have with Oakland Unified District’s Special Education Department (OUSD SPED). We are working with Piedmonter Chantal Guite of Oakland School District to design and fabricate assistive devices for students with a variety of mobility and special needs. My name is Ilana. I’m a mechanical lead of 8033 and a sophomore at Lick Wilmerding High School in San Francisco. I was able to make this project an independent study at my school. This means that I have been getting school credit for this important work and I am able to commit more time to what I am passionate about. Being on the robotics team and working in the Mary G. Ross engineering lab at PHS, I have learned a lot of engineering skills that apply to this project. To start, I use my ability to visualize and prototype before I get to final solutions. This is helpful because the students have very individualized needs – one size doesn’t fit Oakland Unified School District’s 3D printer From CAD to real life all. I have to do a lot of testing to see what will work for each student. Then, I design a 3D model in CAD so we can fabricate using our laser cutter and 3D printers, depending on the project. My teammates started working by making over 20 custom iPad communication guides and clips for kids who are non-verbal and have mobility challenges. The plastic sheets clip onto the devices and guide the student’s fingers to the correct screen button, allowing them to communicate with their teachers and each other. This year, we have expanded the project by making six more key guides, but we have also branched out to help with many other projects. We created a case for what is called a Blue2, essentially a highly intelligent bluetooth button that can be used for many things such as accessing a computer. We designed and fabricated over 25 Blue2 cases. Beyond that, I helped teach several occupational therapists how to use their 3D printer so they can fabricate devices themselves. So far, they have made a toy hearing aid so students that have a hearing aid can use one for their toy. Blue2 Case with student name inscribed Adapting toys for Special Ed students We are excited to be working on a new project with Oakland School District, creating a toy library of adapted toys. Highland Robotics team members are able to modify toys for families with special needs at a much lower price than publicly available. For many of these kids, the only way to interact with toys is via a button, which they click in various ways such as tapping it with their head or knee. Although it is a relatively simple process, adapted toys can be anywhere from 5 to 10 times the price of their unadapted counterparts, making it difficult for lower income families to provide their kids with these modified toys. So far, Highlander Robotics has adapted over 25 toys with hopes of making more. A GoFundMe has been created for this project so that we can buy more materials and toys to adapt. We will also be collecting gently used electronic toys in a bin outside the engineering lab at PHS. To qualify as electric, the toys should be powered by batteries or plug in to a wall outlet. More information is available at (tinyurl.com/p4r5tuy8). All adapted toys will be donated to families through the Oakland School District’s Special Education Dept If you have questions, contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.com. As a community-based team, we do not receive any funding from school which makes sponsorships essential for our success. We appreciate any form of support, whether it is monetary, food, or materials. This money will support us in building a financially sustainable engineering program. Donations may be made at https://www.piedmontmakers.org/. All donations are tax deductible. To learn more, see www.frc8033.com for the sponsorship packet. For sponsorship inquiries, contact Larraine Seiden at lms@larraineseiden. com. articles.text: In a rematch of last year’s Div. 3 North Coast Section quarterfinals, Piedmont got the job done in similar fashion with a 64-51 win over the Analy Tigers of Sebastopol in the season-opening game at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, November 25. PHS dominated the first quarter and jumped out to a 21-8 lead. The score was 36-22 at halftime and increased to 49-33 in the third quarter before Analy put up 18 points in the fourth quarter. The game provided a suggestion of what Piedmont may look like once it’s clicking on all cylinders; a team that can use its size to grab rebounds, move the ball quickly up court, and utilize its athleticism to make quick cuts to the basket. “We’re young but also old in a sense we have seven seniors. But we’re inexperienced. You can see the flashes of brilliance, but you can also see the mistakes we make. We got the lead up to 20 points, but started committing some turnovers, and the lead was quickly back down to 13. We can score quickly and score in bunches, it’s just a matter of whether we can take care of the basketball,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We’ve been working since the loss to Branson last March. I think we’ll have a different look this year with multiple guys scoring Staff Photos Brit Burden had a double-double with 14 points, 12 rebounds, and six assists against Analy. over 10-15 points a game. It will be a more well-rounded attack which will help us deeper into the season. We have guys who can come off the bench as well,” added senior leader Brit Burden. It proved to be a big game for Ravi Silverberg, who scored 22 points including four 3-pointers, a career high for the junior guard. “It’s good to get the win,” acknowledged Silverberg. “It wasn’t perfect, but it’s the first game of the season, so it’s about getting on track. I got some shots up before the game and was feeling good. The threes started falling in the first quarter and after that, the rest of the game felt easy.” Coach Spencer made the deciGuard Ravi Silverberg knocked down 22 points with four 3-pointers. Sophomore Dillon Casey made a big impact with 14 points against Analy. sion to switch Silverberg to the shooting guard role after appearing as a point guard last year. It’s a switch Spencer feels matched Silverberg’s skill set and is making a difference in practice. In Saturday’s game, Silverberg showcased some of those skills in his new spot. “I think I can play any position coach wants me to play. I feel comfortable as shooting guard or point guard, I felt comfortable today, so it was good,” Silverberg added. The game also marked sophomore guard Dillon Casey’s varsity debut, and it was a big one. He finished with 12 points and eight rebounds. “He gets to practice and hour before everyone and is getting up shots. He’s always working and playing club basketball. He’s ready for the moment and will play a big role for us,” said Burden. Piedmont now looks ahead to hosting its West Coast Preps Winter Classic tournament this weekend from Thursday through Saturday, November 30 to December 2. The Highlanders converted five 3-pointers, including three by Silverberg, one by Alex Anderson, and one by Casey. In the second quarter, PHS put up 15 points with four different scorers, including Linnane, Burden and Silverberg each scoring four points while Casey hit a 3-pointer. It was another back-and-forth third quarter with PHS scoring 13 points and allowing 11.. Analy outscored Piedmont 18-15 in the fourth quarter, with 3-pointers by Cash Panico and Casey. Final stats: Burden scored 14 points, 12 rebounds, and six assists. Silverberg scored 22 points and two assists. Casey scored 14 points and grabbed eight rebounds. Linnane had eight points, seven boards. Panico and Anderson scored three, Anderson also had an assist. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team returns after winning last year’s League and North Coast Section titles. Piedmont’s defending Western Alameda County Conference and Division 4 North Coast Section championship team is back in action for the 2023-24 season. The Highlanders return to the court with a significantly different roster. Natalia Martinez, the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year, is the only returning starter from last year’s championship team. “Obviously, it’s going to be different. I feel like we’re up for that challenge,” said coach Bryan Gardere, now in his __ season. Gardere has the task of rebuilding a team without four of its five starters. Trinity Zamora, Eva Levingston, Maddie Hill, and Perseas Gioukaris graduated in May. Zamora and Hill played alongside Martinez for the past three years. “It’s definitely different than the last three years, but the girls we have are amazing,” said Martinez. “People have been stepping up into their roles.” Martinez recently committed to San Diego State and has continued to fine-tune her game well ahead of entering college next fall. “Nat has taken her game to another level,” said Gardere. “She’s finishing with contact, has put more time in the weight room, and is looking at the bigger picture. She knows she wants to have a big senior year but also wants to be ready for the next level in college,” said Gardere. Returning to the team roster is three-year varsity players Kat Melian and Shakila Zuberi. Melian is a tall forward, who is a two-sport athlete with water polo. Zuberi is a guard who has shown good defensive skills and can knock down 3-pointers. “Kat scored a ton of goals in water polo and is coming to basketball with a great mindset. She’s one of the toughest kids I’ve coached in all my years. She puts on a smile and works. You need players like her on your team,” said Gardere. “Kat Melian has been incredible,” added Martinez. “She’s stepped up tremendously to help out this team.” Samantha Smith enters her second year on the team and is Natalia Martinez, the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year, returns for her senior season on the basketball team. articles.text: 2021 PHS grad also wins Turkey Trot with record time It’s been an epic month for Piedmont 2022 graduate Jack Stein. The Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2022, now a sophomore at Pomona-Pitzer, just helped his college reach the highest achievement in its sport by winning the Division 3 NCAA Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 18 in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Stein helped the Sagehens defeat Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, as Pomona’s fifth-best runner. His time of 25:49.3 was the difference in scoring to give his team another national title. “This year I had the pleasure of joining the travel team with the top-10 guys on the team. The Nationals course was in Pennsylvania and we weren’t ranked really high going into it. It was a crazy race and super hilly, but with our veteran experience, we had a good shot of scoring high. We beat University of Wisconsin-La Crosse by one point. Every point really mattered. It’s such an honor to be Division 3 National Champions. We worked hard for it,” said Stein. Coming into Pomona-Pitzer, Stein had to earn his stripes around an older group which won the national title in 2021 before his arrival. “Our seniors were a part of that 2021 team when they were sophomores. It’s good to have senior leadership and people to look up to, especially in running. Just having mentors and a veteran class completely changed the game in terms of improving,” said Stein. But there was more excitement to come for Stein. He returned home for Thanksgiving and not only won the Turkey Trot, he set a new course record of 15:30 on the 5K course on city streets. “It’s a special course. We ran it in high school and I was trained on that course. There’s a couple of hills that the cross country team does hill-reps on, I’ve ran up those hills hundreds of times. It’s special to me… It’s always nice to come home and be surrounded by friends and family,” said Stein. Setting records is nothing new for him. Upon graduation, he left Piedmont High as the school’s all-time record holder in the 3200 meters with a time of 9:12.62, and also set a new school record in the 1600 meters with a time of 4:14.77. He came back to the Turkey Trot surrounded by an all-star cast of Piedmont alums, including Class of 2023 graduates Christian Taylor and Parker Long, and 2018 grad Walter Teitelbaum. “It was good to be back and see a lot of my teammates from high school who are running in college now. It was great to see Christian Taylor (UC Davis) and Parker Long (Cal Poly), and race with them again. I talked to Walter Teitelbaum, who graduated from UC Santa Cruz. He’s someone I’ve been in contact with. “I was excited to come back and race with them. Of course, you want to win the hometown race, especially after winning the National Championship. I was just feeling really confident. It puts a cap on a terrific month of November for the Stein household with younger brother George Stein, a senior at PHS, leading the water polo team to its first North Coast Section championship. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, November 29, 2023 Piedmont’s championship girls’ basketball team is back with a new cast Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team returns after winning last year’s League and North Coast Section titles. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s defending Western Alameda County Conference and Division 4 North Coast Section championship team is back in action for the 2023-24 season. The Highlanders return to the court with a significantly different roster. Natalia Martinez, the Post’s 2023 Athlete of the Year, is the only returning starter from last year’s championship team. “Obviously, it’s going to be different. I feel like we’re up for that challenge,” said coach Bryan Gardere, now in his __ season. Gardere has the task of rebuilding a team without four of its five starters. Trinity Zamora, Eva Levingston, Maddie Hill, and Perseas Gioukaris graduated in May. Zamora and Hill played alongside Martinez for the past three years. “It’s definitely different than the last three years, but the girls we have are amazing,” said Martinez. “People have been stepping up into their roles.” Martinez recently committed to San Diego State and has continued to fine-tune her game well ahead of entering college next fall. “Nat has taken her game to another level,” said Gardere. “She’s finishing with contact, has put more time in the weight room, and is looking at the bigger picture. She knows she wants to have a big senior year but also wants to be ready for the next level in college,” said Gardere. Returning to the team roster is three-year varsity players Kat Melian and Shakila Zuberi. Melian is a tall forward, who is a two-sport athlete with water polo. Zuberi is a guard who has shown good defensive skills and can knock down 3-pointers. “Kat scored a ton of goals in water polo and is coming to basketball with a great mindset. She’s one of the toughest kids I’ve coached in all my years. She puts on a smile and works. articles.text: Shotgun Players’ newest Tony Award-winning production, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, is onstage at the Ashby Theatre in Berkeley now through December 17. Written by John Cameron Mitchell and directed by Richard A. Mosqueda, the play is adapted from the off-Broadway theater hit of the same name, later made into a movie in 2001. Hedwig and the Angry Inch follows German emigrant Hedwig, who is the victim of a botched sex-change operation. This version takes place in a seedy dive bar in Berkeley. Hedwig is an internationally ignored song stylist and East German rock ‘n’ roll goddess. This outrageous play is performed by Pangaea Colter as a member of a rock band with a stand-up comedy routine backed by the band. Mosqueda said the inspiration came from the first viewing of the film in a high school English class. “It was a crudely drawn animation played on the screen detailing a story about the origin of humans, originally three genders, who were once attached and then separated, now looking for the other half. An androgynous blonde bombshell appeared on the screen wailing to the heavens. I was glued to the television. And as a deeply closeted queer kid, I felt seen, if only for a moment,” Mosqueda said. Lyrics and music are by Stephen Trask. To view showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default.asp. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s Cinderella Enchanted, based on the 1997 movie, is playing onstage now through December 22. The classic tale of Cinderella is reborn in this play with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis with music conducted by Jessica Igarashi. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” said Davis. The Berkeley Playhouse production offers some more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited about the fact that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and the parallel life they are living. Cinderella is this aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact outside of being married or born into royalty,” Davis said. The cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel, the Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets.

articles.text: SF Jazz will present the Spanish Harlem Orchestra at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium on Friday, December 15. The three-time Grammy winning Latin jazz band makes its debut at SF Jazz, bringing a repertoire of holiday favorites with a touch of salsa picante. Spanish Harlem Orchestra was founded by producer Aaron Levinson and Puerto Rican pianist and musician Oscar Hernandez. Its debut album was released in 2022. The New York-style band has toured worldwide with jazz greats Chick Corea and Joe Lovano. Their most recent release, Anniversary, featuring trumpeter Randy Brecker, was a winner at this year’s 61st Annual Grammy Awards. The orchestra includes Mitch Frohman on saxophone and flute, Manuel Ruiz and Alex Norris on trumpet, Doug Beavers and Juanga Lakunza on trombone, Gerardo Madera on bass, George Delgado on congas, Luisito Quintero on timbales, Jorge Gonzalez on percussion, and vocalists Jeremy Bosch Marco Bermudez and Carlos Cascante. The performance at SF Jazz begins at 7:30 p.m. Tickets are available at https:// www.sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/spanish-harlem-orchestra/. articles.text: Piedmont gemologist in 2-part illustrated jewelry lecture Piedmont resident and gemologist Sacha Grippando will present a two-part on the jewelry collections of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor. Titled a Legacy of Love, the first talk will take place on Friday, December 8 at 6 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Art, 801 Magnolia Avenue. The two lectures will be a survey of retro and mid-century jewelry with a focus on the jewelry collection of the Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor from the years 1935-1960. Jewelry from that era is bold, Photos by Cecil Beaton Wallace Simpson, the Duchess of Windsor, was always elegantly dressed. Photos by Cecil Beaton The Duke and Duchess of Windsor. Gemologist Sacha Grippando colorful and extravagant. The Duchess of Windsor and Elizabeth Taylor each amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones as well as innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were acquired as gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. These lectures will examine these two exceptional ladies, their fascinating and scandalous lives, and of course their fabulous jewelry. The first lecture will explore in depth the jewelry collection of Wallis Simpson, the Duchess of Windsor. The second part of this survey is scheduled for Thursday evening, February 1, 2024, and will offer details of the collection of American actress Elizabeth Taylor. Both lectures will begin at 6 p.m. and will be a little more than one hour. They will be followed by light refreshments. Donations are encouraged, and both events are open to all.

articles.text: Part Six in a series Because movies are so deeply embedded in our culture, we have included their titles and stories as familiar referents. Some are animated, others are portrayals of real life, both filled with a kind of magic. More than a few have become iconic. However, we are likely not as familiar with the countless individuals who write the narratives, create the characters, and oversee the productions. Watch the credits at the end of any film and you get a sense of the extraordinary number of people involved. Animation clearly relies on the engine of imagination while creating characters and worlds and narratives that are extraordinary and involve a kind of… magic. To successfully capture and hold the attention of young audiences is no small thing. articles.text: The golden age of comic books – the 1940s – was launched well before television appeared in living rooms, when that now familiar, almost eerie luminescent glow fills living room windows on any given evening. Growing up, I loved comics, as did my friends. We all had stacks in our rooms, most read until the staples gave way, the pulpy paper dog-eared, their thin spines taped. I kept a china dish in my dresser drawer filled with dimes and nickels saved from my paper route. They were next to my skate key and a dusty, well-oiled Spaulding outfielder’s glove. The comics we coveted were, in the main, wonderfully drawn stories about superheroes: Superman, Batman, Spider Man, and, one of my favorites, Straight Arrow. I recall for a time that I treasured any comic featuring Captain Marvel, published at the time (between 1940 and 1953) by Fawcett comics. They featured a young radio reporter, Billy Batson, who, when he said Shazam! morphed into Captain Marvel, outfitted in latex, a lightning bolt on his chest, an orange cape with a bolt down the back. Like most heroes, he had super powers, could fly faster than anything and shoot lightning bolts from his hands. Fawcett lost its Captain Marvel copyright to DC comics who, in the 1960s, revived the hero, calling him Captain Marvel…but that’s another story. The film Shazam!, released in 2019 is based on the Fawcett version I knew and loved. The film is an origin story, always interesting, and in my opinion best when lots of screen time is devoted to the kids/young teens instead of the adults. Billy Batson (Asher Angel), 14-years old, is in search of his mother. He has been bouncing from foster home to the streets and then back for most of his young life and, not surprisingly, has abandonment issues. He longs for a family and feels intensely and rebelliously alone. When, through a series of circumstances, he is given Shazam! powers, his superhero alter ego, played by Zachary Levi, seems jarringly out of synch with young street-smart Billy, who has knocked around for most of his life. I was disappointed every time Billy said Shazam!. Act three is filled with CGI explosions, all focused on the story’s villain, Dr. Thaddeus Sivana (Mark Strong), who has extraordinary super powers. As a character, he seems a bit silly and tedious and the blow-out battles between Billy/Shazam and Sivana go on way too long, They end with all the kids living in the foster home abruptly transformed into superheroes, none as interesting as the foster kids themselves. By then, I lost interest. Shazam! Directed by David F. Sandberg. Starring Zachery Levi, Mark Strong, Asher Angel. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Zachary Levi as Captain Marvel in Shazam!

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Flipped is set in white suburbia and spans those now iconic years of the late 50s and early 60s. For filmmakers doing a period re-creation, the cars have fins, millions are moving to the suburbs, and the music is a cresting wave of rock and roll, featuring memorable signature songs that filled countless gyms during Friday night sock hops. If you grew up during that time, it’s tempting to believe that no generation before or since experienced anything quite like it. It was a gestalt of culture and change. The soundtrack to that period was Elvis and Buddy, Bill Haley and the Comets, Chubby Checker and the Big Bopper, all leading the way followed by a long line of groups and stand alone singers. Politically, it was the Cold War, the ever-present scimitar of nuclear weapons, and it’s not a stretch to say that if there was a moment when it all ended, it would be in early November 1963 with the assassination of John F, Kennedy. One of the best films that capture this time period George Lucas’ American Graffiti, followed by Rob Reiner’s Stand by Me. Both films are remarkable in that they tell compelling teen stories filled with magic. Because Reiner demonstrated such a deft touch with Stand by Me, seeming to understand reflexively that universal transition called “coming of age,” the expectation was that he would bring the same authentic insight to Flipped. The story is adapted from a contemporary teen novel by Wendelin Van Draanen and hugely popular in 2001. Flipped begins with Juli (Madeline Carroll) and Bryce (Callan McAuliffe), both second graders, who meet when Bryce moves into the neighborhood. Juli is immediately smitten. Bryce is repelled, her being a girl and all. The story soon focuses on how they navigate middle school and Bryce drolly points out that he has spent half a decade avoiding Juli, intimidated by her expressions of affection. She has spent that time resolutely reaching out and being rebuffed. But all of that is about to be upended, meaning flipped. Though there is a nice contrast between the families – Bryce’s is upwardly mobile and somewhat affluent, and Julie’s is working class and outwardly poor – not much is made of these differences and how they impact the two budding adolescents. There’s joy and pain in this story, but Reiner holds back on both counts. He seems content to settle for “nice.” That isn’t the adjective that comes to mind when thinking of Stand by Me. There are truths in this movie, though Reiner, who co-wrote the screenplay, doesn’t explore them. One nugget in Flipped is John Mahoney, a superb character actor, who portrays Bryce’s grandfather in a role that demonstrates the breadth and depth of Mahoney’s talent. He has appeared in supporting roles over the years, and his presence in Flipped is worth the price of admission. If you have a tween sitting on the sofa, already worried that since school is fully underway and all the really cool movies of summer past are long gone, suggest that said grumpy gremlin consider Flipped. It is a sweet movie. Flipped. Directed By Rob Reiner. Starring Calan McAuliffe, Madeline Carroll, and Rebecca DeMournay. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Born Paul Bernard Lahaderne on December 5, 1947 in San Francisco, Paul was the son of Bernard Lahaderne and Mary Traynor. He, his sister, Denise, and his brother, Bob, grew up in a loving multigenerational home on Ashbury Street in the City. Paul often spoke of his childhood, and with great affection and appreciation for his parents whose hard work and sense of family would shape and guide his life. Paul attended St. Agnes School and Saint Ignatius High School. As with his childhood, there were many stories of his high school days. Paul took great pride in his football years at S.I. under Coach Vince Tringali. Paul graduated from University of San Francisco. While attending school, he worked nights and summers to finance his education. He then went on to Hastings College of the Law. Before beginning his legal career, Paul served in the U.S. Army on active duty at Fort Benning, Georgia, followed by the Army Reserve. He retired with the rank of Captain. He went on to have a distinguished career as an attorney. After starting his career at CalTrans, Paul moved to Sedgwick, Detert, Moran and Arnold. For 20 years he was a member of the American Board of Trial Advocates. In 1986, Paul met Teresa Craigie and they married in 1989. They have two sons, Peter and Jack Lahaderne. Paul was a devoted husband and a loving and supportive father. Whether it was driving all over northern California for Peter’s baseball games or building an easel for Jack’s paintings, Paul was a consistent and positive presence in their lives. Paul was also active in the Piedmont community and many knew him from his involvement in youth sports. From coaching the Bruisers soccer team, to serving as President of Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation, to assisting with the Piedmont High School baseball team, he always enjoyed contributing his time. Although it must be admitted that Piedmont resident Paul Lahaderne died on October 28. as a soccer coach he was far more gifted at being a role model and keeping the team in line than with his knowledge of soccer. Paul was beloved by his family, who will dearly miss him and his oft-told stories. He is survived by his wife, Teresa, and sons, Peter and Jack Lahaderne; sister DeeDee Dagemjian; sisters-inlaw Mary Craigie, Ellen Craigie, and Jennifer Craigie; brother-inlaw Peter Craigie (Conna McCarthy); nieces and nephews Kieran Craigie, Cormac Craigie (Lauren Craigie) Kathlyn Craigie, Matthew Bonini (Chelsea Bonini), Vincent Bonini, Robert Lahaderne (Michele Lahaderne), Jonathan Lahaderne (Rebekka Lahaderne), and Martha Lahaderne. Paul also leaves behind a large extended family, as well as many friends, neighbors and colleagues; all knowing Paul’s best story was not the one he told, but the one he lived. A Catholic memorial service will be held on December 8 at 5:00 p.m. at Corpus Christi Catholic Church, 322 St. James Drive in Piedmont. A memorial reception will be at 6:15 p.m. at the Claremont Hotel, 41 Tunnel Road in Berkeley. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial contributions be made to The Tringali Scholarship at St Ignatius College Prep, 2001 37th Avenue, San Francisco CA 94116, or a charity of choice.

The group included Christine Calliste, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, Dottie Hutch, Priscilla Wanerus, Karin Fetherston, Lisa Euphrat, Judy Love, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kuo, Joanne Larson, Mimi Engle, Kathy Rolfson, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Sharona Fischrup, Chuck Oraftik, Marj Blackman, Nava Shahan, Melba Yee, Carol Lyons, Stella Houston, Russ Nelson, Kat Lang, Edith Lee, Martin Levy, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, Irene Thompson, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Claudine Bach was walking with them for the first time, and that Melba Yee’s sister, Pansy Yee, was there for a Thanksgiving visit. It was Thanksgiving Eve and members of the Walking on Wednesdays group were where they always are at 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday mornings – in front of the Exedra. It was a lovely morning and 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend were there to enjoy the weather, being together, and work on their Thanksgiving dinner appetites. They knew 2,400 runners and walkers were going to be on this very spot the next morning for the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The Wednesday walkers were there to get a head start on them and one day before Thanksgiving, be the first across the finish line. Thanks were shared for the friendships that have come from this walking group, and some Thanksgiving race information was shared. According to “Run Signup,” over 750,000 Americans participated in a turkey trot last Thanksgiving in one of over 730 races across the U.S. The Piedmont Turkey Trot is conducted by an independent non-profit that supports the high school cross-country and track and field teams and the PHS Boosters. This was the 22nd year for the Piedmont Turkey Trot which started in 2001 with 300 runners. Participation has been as high as 3,100 one year. The number of runners was capped at 2,400 this year. Awards are given for the top three male and female finishers in 10 separate age categories, from 13 and under to age 80 and over. Last year’s overall winner was Walter Teitelbaum, a PHS grad, who completed the 5-kilometer course in 16 minutes and two seconds. The walkers did not think they would challenge Walter’s time, but they looked forward to walking the entire Turkey Trot route of 3.1 miles. It was agreed that the walker who finished the course first would be declared the Wednesday Walkers’ winner. Even though the Turkey Trot banner was not yet up at the start & finish line on Magnolia Avenue, the walkers got a fast start anyway, going on Highland Avenue to Wildwood. A homeowner must have thought the walkers needed to be cooled off because their sprinkler was showering the sidewalk. The group stepped around the water, took a left on Wildwood Avenue, then a right on Crocker and Lafayette Avenues, and onto La Salle Avenue. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors celebrated their 27th Anniversary on September 27th with a special luncheon at the Piedmont Community Hall. The organization was founded in 1996 by Lois Dawers and with the encouragement of Mark Delventhal, the long-time Director of Recreation, the Piedmont Seniors was established. Fifty people were in attendance for the anniversary festivities, Guests included members of the Police and Fire Departments, as well as Recreation staff members. The lunch was catered by Ann’s Catering of Berkeley. Police Chief Bowers, Fire Chief Brannigan and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen offered remarks about current events in Piedmont and their support by the Piedmont Seniors. Before the luncheon the group was fortunate to have Gail Lombardi, President of the Piedmont Historical Society, provide a special presentation about Piedmont’s history, with a slideshow of what early Piedmont looked like. She mentioned the Piedmont Hotel, which is now part of Piedmont Park, and the therapeutic springs which attracted many people to the Piedmont hills at the beginning of the twentieth century. In the 1860s, the discovery of sulphur springs began to attract visitors to Piedmont. Mineral springs were believed to possess great curative powers, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel, built by Walter Blair, opened in 1871 to provide accommodations for those who came to “take the waters.” Built on the site of today’s Exedra, this grand hotel had a wide veranda, 20 bedrooms and 2 suites, 5 dining rooms, and a Grand Saloon with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, and pot-bellied stove (for men only). The hotel thrived until 1892 when, at 9:15 a.m. on November 17, the hotel came to a sudden end when a fire in the chimney expanded to the roof. It was not until 11:30 a.m. that Chemical Engine #1 arrived from Oakland to contain the fire. Newspapers reported that “the absence of any water supply left the occupants of the doomed building no other recourse than to sit down in the shade and watch the building burn.” Piedmont became an official city in California in 1907, for two main reasons: people wanted to escape the ravages of the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco, and they wanted to become an entity separate from Oakland. The Piedmont Seniors group meets monthly on the fourth Wednesday at the Piedmont Community Hall at 10 a.m. They also go on monthly excursions to a variety of locations throughout the Greater Bay Area. articles.text: Staying healthy during the holidays can be challenging, especially when there are lots of activities to participate in and meals filled with sweet treats. Even though the excursions and dietary changes during the holidays bring joy, they could also potentially be disruptive for seniors. Here are five ways to help ensure that seniors enjoy a happy and healthy holiday season. 1. Provide healthy snack options The holidays can often be a time to indulge in food. To offset the decadent foods and goodies people eat during this time of year, be sure to offer healthy snack options too. This can be anything from almonds or walnuts covered with cinnamon or holiday spices, to bowls of seasonal fruit such as fresh cranberries. You can also serve lighter meals (such as soup or chili made with ground turkey) throughout the day when you know a big dinner is planned for the evening. You still want your loved ones to be able to enjoy their favorite foods at this time of year, so the key is trying to provide balance in the meals surrounding those big holiday feasts. 2. Drink Lots of Water It can be easy to forget to drink water amid the hustle and bustle of the holidays. However, staying hydrated is essential to remaining healthy. You can help protect the seniors in your life by making sure water is easily accessible for them. If an elderly adult is coming to stay with you for the holidays, make sure you keep their room stocked with water bottles. Additionally, make sure you have water bottles available in the car and your purse while running those holiday errands or going to family gatherings. 3. Exercise The cold weather can make us want to stay cozy inside and may make the thought of exercise seem daunting. Exercise doesn’t need to involve an intense routine though – even just a simple walk around the block can provide mental and physical benefits for seniors. Walking around the neighborhood can also allow you and your loved one to have some quality time together, enjoying Christmas lights or other sights of the season. If it is too cold or rainy to go for a walk outside, consider going to the mall and walking a few laps around your favorite stores. Staying active and keeping your body moving at a calm rate is a great way to help your parents and grandparents stay healthy. 4. Get Plenty of Rest Try to make sure that your loved one has time to rest during the day and gets a good night’s sleep in the evening. Maintaining a good sleep schedule and regular bedtime is very important, especially for seniors who may get tired and worn out more easily during this time of year. If your parent or grandparent has traveled a long way to see you, it is even more critical that you find time for them to rest throughout the day. Once your loved one has arrived, offer to watch a holiday movie, enjoy a cup of hot cocoa, listen to Christmas music, or read a book with them, rather than diving into a day of busy activities. 5. Offer to host Sometimes enter taining guests and cooking a large meal can be overwhelming for seniors. If an older relative is the one who usually hosts a family gathering, offer to take that responsibility off their plate this year, especially if it is a source of stress. If your relative enjoys hosting, make sure you offer to help them by taking care of decorating or cleaning up after the event is over. You can also search for ways to make holiday preparations simpler for your loved one, such as suggesting that the family participating in a white elephant gift exchange or secret Santa style gift giving. This may help your older relative because they will only need to focus on purchasing one gift instead of buying presents for the entire family. Maintaining healthy practices this holiday season and being flexible when it comes to traditions will allow seniors to enjoy healthy and happy holidays with their loved ones. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors pay tribute to Bosco the dog, Sunol’s former mayor, by visiting a statue erected in his honor. Pictured are Edith Hereso (left), Sue Getreuer, Gregory Jurin, Nancy Hinsch, Janet Epstein, Jim Ayotte, Mona Jamieson, Fred Pemberton, Larry Hu, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Tanya Hu. Not pictured: Larry and Patti Singer. Fourteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group went on a round-trip scenic train ride through Niles Canyon to the historic town of Sunol. Their first stop was in front of the old Post Office to see the statue of Sunol’s former mayor, Bosco, a black Labrador Retriever and Rottweiler. Bosco defeated two humans to win the honorary mayoral election in 1981 and served until his death in 1994. A statue was later erected in his honor in 2008. Bosco even appeared as a contestant on the game show “3rd Degree” where the panelists failed to guess Bosco’s occupation. The Seniors then embarked on an 80-minute diesel train ride on the Niles Canyon Railway. This train is a living museum preserving an era of California’s railroad history as the last segment of the original Transcontinental Railroad to San Francisco. The Niles Canyon Railway is operated solely by volunteer members of the Pacific Locomotive Association, whose mission is “to develop and operate a working railroad museum for the benefit of the general public.” The Niles Canyon Railway also has an informative museum on the grounds depicting the important role of Chinese laborers in the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad. The station was built in 1996 and the oldest rail car dates from 1915. In 1988 The Pacific Locomotive Association brought railroad passenger operation back to life in Niles Canyon. The Association wanted to preserve the atmosphere of railroads in small-town America before the 1960s by connecting the historic communities of Sunol, the Niles District of Fremont and eventually Pleasanton. The Association’s goal is to educate the public in railroad history, tradition, and the evolution of all transportation technology. Since the Niles Canyon Railway heavily relies on donations, it has an annual fundraiser at the holiday time, called “The Tree of Lights.” This is an enchanting holiday excursion filled with music, cheer, refreshments, and features holiday lights, decorations, and even a visit by Santa Claus. This has been an annual destination for many Bay Area families for more than 10 years, with steam and diesel trains departing from both Niles and Sunol stations, however this popular trip is currently sold out for 2023. After a relaxing trip between Sunol and Niles, the group worked up an appetite. Returning to Dublin, they enjoyed a delicious Italian lunch at the Dublin restaurant, Frankie, Johnnie & Luigi Too. This restaurant has quite an extensive menu, and no one left hungry as ample portions were available for all. For more information about meetings and excursions of the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov. Meetings are usually held on the fourth Wednesday of each month from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall in Piedmont Park. articles.text: Dear MacMama: I want to buy a new laptop for travel. I have a 2021 iMac that is my main computer. I have thought about an iPad, but have decided on a laptop, since I often have to work when I am away. My main work is spreadsheets and documents. There are so many options, I can’t make heads or tails of the different laptops. What would you suggest? —Marjorie, Oakland Dear Marjorie: I’m glad you told me what tasks you mainly do on your computer. One thing I don’t know is how much space you need, so I’m going to make some suggestions with some variations. I’m assuming that you keep most of your files on your main computer, your 2021 iMac. In a perfect world, these files would be in sync with your travel computer also. So, I’m going to suggest that you make sure that you are syncing your files with iCloud. Very likely, your photos are already synced through iCloud, meaning when you take a picture on your iPhone, it automatically shows up on your computer. And you should be doing the same in your position with your desktop and document files. If you do this on both machines, they will both stay in sync for the work that you must do. Note that iCloud has a setting called “optimize Mac storage” which will store local copies (on your Mac) of files that have been accessed recently if your Mac has enough space. If you’re running out of space on your Mac, it will automatically move files as needed to iCloud. One of the downsides of this is if you haven’t opened a file for a while, and it has been stored in iCloud, and you are in a place with your new laptop that doesn’t have a good internet connection, you will not have access to this file. This can be turned on and off in your System Settings/Apple ID/iCloud. Note that turning this off will start to download all files you have stored in iCloud onto your Mac that are not already there. I often turn this setting off before I travel, so I have access to everything. It’s a good idea to make sure that you have iCloud set to sync your documents before you set up a new machine. As you noticed, there are two types of laptops for sale each with many possibilities of customization, MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. For your purposes, I would suggest a 13” or 15” MacBook Air with an M2 processor, 8 or 16GB RAM, with at least the same size hard drive that your iMac has. Likely a 512 GB Solid State Drive (SSD) is fine, but it might be safer to get a 1 TB SSD. You don’t need a lot of processing power for spreadsheets and documents. But you can no longer upgrade your hard drive or RAM, so it’s best to think ahead and get a machine that you will not outgrow. If you bought a 13 inch MacBook Air with 8 GB RAM and a 1 TB SSD, it would cost $1399 before tax and not including any sales or promotions. A 15-inch Air with the same specs is, $1699. If you told me that you were going to be editing pictures, music or movies, my answer would be very different. In that case you need as much RAM and processing power that you can afford. To give you an example, I would steer you either to get the same machine with 24 GB Ram, $1799 for the 13 inch and $2099 for the 15 inch. Or even better, a MacBook Pro with one of the M3 processors. There are three to choose from. For most folks, the M3 is fine, the M3 Pro is even better, and the M3 Max is overkill. As I said, if you’re doing things that take a lot of processing power, using Final Cut Pro or Adobe After Effects, then the M3 max processor is something you will greatly appreciate. Let’s just look at a couple of those models to see the price difference. A 14 inch MacBook Pro with the basic M3 Pro processor, 18 GB unified memory and a 1 TB SSD will run $2199 before tax. Choose the better M3 Pro processor, bring the memory up to 36GB, and it jumps to $2799. For most content creators, photo and music editors this is plenty. For people who really need (or just like to have the best), the 14 inch MacBook Pro with the most loaded M3 Max processor, 48 GB unified memory, and 1 TB SSD, you are at $3699. And I haven’t even said a thing about the 16 inch MacBook Pro. So, you see it’s really easy to go down the rabbit hole with all of the specifics. But if you’re only working on documents, sending some emails doing light photo editing, the MacBook Air is a great choice. Apple has not provided the MacBook Air with the M3 processor yet, but they probably will. There won’t be enough of a difference between the M2 and the M3 to have you wait. As example, I have a 13 inch MacBook Air with the M2 processor, 16 gigs of RAM, and a 2 TB SSD. This is the machine I travel with, even on my photo trips. I use Adobe Lightroom, and I have no trouble with the specs on this machine. If you have enough time, then you can order a laptop with the exact specifics that makes sense to you. If you are traveling very soon, you may be limited to what Apple has in stock. Make sure to check out other retailers like Best Buy, and even B&H Photo or Amazon. pages.text: Wednesday, November 29, 2023 29 Piedmont Seniors visit Sunol by train The Piedmont Seniors pay tribute to Bosco the dog, Sunol’s former mayor, by visiting a statue erected in his honor. Pictured are Edith Hereso (left), Sue Getreuer, Gregory Jurin, Nancy Hinsch, Janet Epstein, Jim Ayotte, Mona Jamieson, Fred Pemberton, Larry Hu, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Tanya Hu. Not pictured: Larry and Patti Singer. By Janet Epstein Fourteen members of the Piedmont Seniors group went on a round-trip scenic train ride through Niles Canyon to the historic town of Sunol. Their first stop was in front of the old Post Office to see the statue of Sunol’s former mayor, Bosco, a black Labrador Retriever and Rottweiler. Bosco defeated two humans to win the honorary mayoral election in 1981 and served until his death in 1994. A statue was later erected in his honor in 2008. Bosco even appeared as a contestant on the game show “3rd Degree” where the panelists failed to guess Bosco’s occupation. The Seniors then embarked on an 80-minute diesel train ride on the Niles Canyon Railway. This train is a living museum preserving an era of California’s railroad history as the last segment of the original Transcontinental Railroad to San Francisco. The Niles Canyon Railway is operated solely by volunteer members of the Pacific Locomotive Association, whose mission is “to develop and operate a working railroad museum for the benefit of the general public.” The Niles Canyon Railway also has an informative museum on the grounds depicting the important role of Chinese laborers in the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad. The station was built in 1996 and the oldest rail car dates from 1915. In 1988 The Pacific Locomotive Association brought railroad passenger operation back to life in Niles Canyon. The Association wanted to preserve the atmosphere of railroads in small-town America before the 1960s by connecting the historic communities of Sunol, the Niles District of Fremont and eventually Pleasanton. The Association’s goal is to educate the public in railroad history, tradition, and the evolution of all transportation technology. Since the Niles Canyon Railway heavily relies on donations, it has an annual fundraiser at the holiday time, called “The Tree of Lights.” This is an enchanting holiday excursion filled with music, cheer, refreshments, and features holiday lights, decorations, and even a visit by Santa Claus. This has been an annual destination for many Bay Area families for more than 10 years, with steam and diesel trains departing from both Niles and Sunol stations, however this popular trip is currently sold out for 2023. After a relaxing trip between Sunol and Niles, the group worked up an appetite. Returning to Dublin, they enjoyed a delicious Italian lunch at the Dublin restaurant, Frankie, Johnnie & Luigi Too. This restaurant has quite an extensive menu, and no one left hungry as ample portions were available for all. For more information about meetings and excursions of the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov. Meetings are usually held on the fourth Wednesday of each month from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall in Piedmont Park. pages.text: Wednesday, November 29, 2023 31 Scout Tree Lot Continued from page 9 “It’s fun to be here,” said Abe Shrago, a Tiger Scout from Pack 5, in his first year volunteering at the tree lot. Despite being one of the youngest Scouts on shift last weekend, he had one of the most important jobs – transporting trees to the checkout counter using a tree dolly larger than he was tall. “I’m just so grateful. People loved me for picking their trees out this weekend. It makes me feel happy,” said Shrago. Equally happy were the many customers that the Scouts helped. Customer Elena McCormick had many of her questions answered by a helpful Webelos Scout. Leo Shrago, Abe’s brother, helped her decide which tree would be best for her home. “After talking to Leo, we decided to get a Douglas fir tree this year,” said McCormick. “Hopefully the needles won’t fall too much, because we have a cat at home who will be enjoying his first Christmas.” After buying a Christmas tree at the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot, Sankalp Sharma watches as Nuala Price helps him lash it to the top of his car. Mike Beuselinck, the parent of a Cub Scout in Pack 5, carries shears to cut the twine around trees to open them up before being put on customers’ cars. “This is a fantastic event in a beautiful city,” said Thomas McCormick, Elena’s brother who was visiting for the holidays. “It’s super nice to explore the city and find this today.” Proceeds from the lot benefit the nearly 1000 Cub Scouts, Scouts, Venturers, Explorers, and members of the Piedmont Language School, who are all part of the Piedmont Scout Council. For more information, visit: www.scouttreelot.org. Troy Alering, the father of a Scout in Troop 11, helps trim the base of trees at the sawing station at the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot on opening weekend. This is his 11th year helping at the tree lot.
